blocks.text: Preference losses train a model based on relative comparisons between two candidate responses, one preferred over the other, rather than training toward a single fixed correct answer the way cross-entropy loss, covered earlier in this module, does.
This topic closes out the Loss Functions module by introducing the loss family that underlies alignment training, a topic covered in full depth in its own dedicated module later in this course.
1. What Preference Losses Are For
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100771-977984325.png

Every loss function covered earlier in this module assumed a single, known correct target, the right classification label, the right next token, the right token level tag. Preference losses instead assume access to a comparison, given two candidate responses, which one is genuinely better, without necessarily needing to define one single perfect correct answer at all.
2. Beyond Correct vs Incorrect, Better vs Worse

blocks.alt: Beyond Correct vs Incorrect, Better vs Worse
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100773-247397892.png

Some tasks genuinely have more than one reasonable answer, and what matters is not matching one fixed target exactly but producing a response a human would judge as better along dimensions like helpfulness, tone, or safety, exactly the kind of judgment preference losses are designed to train toward.
3. Pairwise Comparison as the Core Idea

blocks.alt: Pairwise Comparison as the Core Idea
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100773-510562692.png

The core training signal for a preference loss is a pair of responses to the same prompt, one marked as chosen, the preferred response, and one marked as rejected, the less preferred one, and the loss pushes the model to make the chosen response more likely and the rejected response less likely relative to each other.
4. The DPO Loss, A Concrete Example

blocks.alt: The DPO Loss, A Concrete Example
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100774-972886952.png

Direct preference optimization, DPO, is one of the most widely used preference loss formulations, directly increasing the model relative probability of the chosen response over the rejected response for the same prompt, without needing a separate reward model, a contrast covered further in the Alignment Training module later in this course.

code.content:
# A conceptual sketch of a preference loss comparison
chosen_log_prob = model.log_probability(prompt, chosen_response)
rejected_log_prob = model.log_probability(prompt, rejected_response)
# The loss encourages chosen_log_prob to rise relative to rejected_log_prob

blocks.text: 5. Preference Losses vs Cross-Entropy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100774-515774369.png

Where cross-entropy loss, covered earlier in this module, measures distance from one fixed correct target, preference loss measures the relative gap between two candidate responses, a fundamentally different training signal better suited to shaping subjective qualities like helpfulness or tone than a single correct answer could ever capture.

blocks.text: 6. Where Preference Data Comes From
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100774-95180082.png

Preference data typically comes from human raters comparing two model generated responses to the same prompt and indicating which one they prefer, an annotation process related to, but distinct from, the labeling covered in the Dataset Annotation topic, since it asks for a relative judgment rather than a single correct label.

blocks.title: This connects to the RLHF terminology used broadly in the field
blocks.content: Reinforcement learning from human feedback, RLHF, and direct preference optimization both rely on this same kind of pairwise human preference data, differing mainly in how that data actually gets used to update the model, a distinction covered in the Alignment Training module.

blocks.text: 7. Preference Losses and Alignment Training
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100775-145828810.png

Preference losses are the specific mechanism alignment training uses to shape a model toward being more helpful, honest, and safe, building on top of a model that has already been supervised fine-tuned, covered earlier in this course, rather than starting from a raw pretrained model.
8. Reading a Preference Loss Value

A decreasing preference loss over training generally indicates the model is increasingly assigning higher relative probability to chosen responses over rejected ones, though, similar to the earlier caution about sequence-to-sequence loss, this training signal is usually paired with separate human or automated evaluation, covered in the Evaluation module, to confirm real world quality improvements.
9. When Preference Losses Are Necessary

Preference losses are specifically necessary when a task genuine goal is subjective quality, tone, helpfulness, safety, rather than matching one objectively correct answer, for tasks with a clear single correct target, classification, extraction, straightforward supervised fine-tuning with cross-entropy remains the more direct, simpler choice.
Worked Example

A team has already supervised fine-tuned a model to answer customer questions correctly, but finds its tone sometimes comes across as overly blunt. Rather than trying to define one single correct polite phrasing for every possible question, they collect pairs of responses to the same questions, one blunt and one warmer in tone, with human raters marking the warmer one as preferred.

Training with a preference loss on this comparison data shifts the model default tone to be warmer across a wide range of questions, a subjective quality improvement that a single correct answer cross-entropy approach would have struggled to capture directly.
Common Mistakes

items: Trying to force a subjective quality like tone into a single correct answer cross-entropy setup instead of using preference data
Collecting preference pairs without clear, consistent guidelines for what makes one response genuinely preferred over another
Assuming a decreasing preference loss alone guarantees improved real world quality without further evaluation
Applying preference training to a raw pretrained model rather than one that has already gone through supervised fine-tuning first

blocks.text: Practice

For a task with a subjective quality dimension, tone, conciseness, or helpfulness, sketch what a chosen versus rejected response pair might look like for the same prompt, confirming you understand the relative comparison structure preference losses are built around.
Key Takeaway

Preference losses train a model using relative comparisons between a chosen and a rejected response rather than a single fixed correct target, making them the right tool for shaping subjective qualities like helpfulness and tone, and they form the specific mechanism behind alignment training, covered in full depth in its own dedicated module later in this course.
